newsitem.title: ABU DHABI: UAE's big arms show opens amid hopes for deals.
newsitem.headline: UAE's big arms show opens amid hopes for deals.

text.p: Sleek-suited men began promoting everything from Czech sub-machineguns with silencers to all-terrain combat vehicles on Sunday as Abu Dhabi opened one of the world's biggest arms shows.

Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Sheikh Khalifa bin Zaid al-Nahayan, one of the powerful men who gives the green light to arms deals in this emirate with an appetite for high-tech hardware, opened the five-day IDEX weapons exhibition by some 750 companies from 53 countries.
He and other senior United Arab Emirates officials looked on as a Ukrainian T-72 main battle tank and other vehicles ploughed through muddy terrain below a grandstand at the opening ceremony.

Weapons makers -- from major names like France's Giat Industries to Greece's Powder and Cartridge Co -- hope to use the event to gain better access to the Gulf Arab arms market, where memories of Iraq's 1990 invasion of Kuwait are still fresh.
George Todd, regional director for the Indiana-based AM General Corp, stood behind his firm's sand-coloured Hummer combat vehicle mounted with machineguns and discussed market prospects.
"We are in talks with all Gulf Arab states as well as countries like Egypt and Jordan and we hope to satisfy their requirements for the Hummer," he said of the vehicle used in the 1991 Gulf War.
"We think this show is very important to the Gulf."
A few feet away, Czech 9mm pistols used by special forces and commandoes were hanging on a wall. In a nearby stand, an electronic guidance device for naval vessels displayed a map of the UAE coast.
In the South African pavilion, a video featured a mine-field breaching system and an anti-rocket device.
As salesmen stood by instruments that deliver destruction with pinpoint accuracy, industry executives awaited deals expected to be announced at IDEX.
Abu Dhabi, nervously watching non-Arab Iran across the Gulf, has emerged as a prized customer in the international arms bazaar and several contracts are expected to be announced at IDEX.

The race with the biggest price tag is between U.S. firm Lockheed Martin Corp and France's Dassault Aviation for a $6 billion deal to sell the UAE up to 80 long-range strike aircraft. Market speculation has for months suggested the UAE will announce its decision during IDEX.
Other possible deals include a contract potentially worth $1 billion to supply the country with fast patrol boats.

Competing firms include Britain's Vosper Thorneycroft Plc, France's DCNI, international arm of the state-owned naval shipyard Direction des Construction Navales, Dutch state-owned Shipyard Koninklijke Schelde Groep and Germany's Lurssen.
Two U.S. firms -- Newport News Shipbuilding and Halter Marine -- are also competing.

The UAE is also moving closer to choosing an air defence missile system in a deal potentially worth between $500 million and $1 billion. U.S. company Raytheon and Russian missile-maker Antei are the contenders.
